It was a spring evening. As the sun sank towards the horizon, it cast red light into the room. The windmill's sails on the embankment swept shadows over walls and windowpanes, passing and returning with monotonous regularity: one moment dark, two moments bright.

Niels Lyhne sat at the window, looking through the embankment's dark, glossy elms towards the burning clouds. He had spent the day in the country, walking beneath flowering beeches, beside green rye-fields, and across meadows bright with flowers. Everything had seemed so light and lovely: the blue sky, the shining Sound, the astonishing beauty of the women he passed. He had sung along the woodland path. Gradually the song lost its words, then its rhythm, then its sound, until a dizzying silence overtook him. Even with his eyes closed he felt his body drinking the light and his nerves quivering in response. Each breath of cool, heady air sent blood racing more fiercely through his trembling, helpless veins. He seemed filled with spring's swarming forces of growth and budding and germination, mysteriously seeking release through him in one enormous cry. He thirsted for that cry and listened for it until listening became a vague, swollen longing.
Sitting now beside the window, he felt that same longing stirring to life again.

He yearned for a thousand shivering dreams, cool and delicate images, translucent colours, vanishing perfumes, exquisite music streaming from silvery strings stretched taut and high. Then silence: its very heart, where no wandering note had ever travelled upon the air, where everything rested as if dead, bathed in the quiet glow of reds and the languorous warmth of burning perfume.—No, this was not what he wanted. But the images drifted out of his mood and drowned everything else until he turned away and resumed his own line of thought.

He was tired of himself, of chilly ideas and dreams made in the brain. Life a poem? Not if you spent it endlessly making poetry out of your own life instead of living. How harmless it all was, and empty, empty, empty! Chasing yourself, slyly tracking your own footprints, inevitably round in circles. Pretending to plunge into life's current while remaining on the bank fishing for yourself, hauling yourself out in one peculiar disguise after another! If only something could overwhelm him—life, passion, love—so that instead of shaping it into poems, he had to let it shape him!

Without thinking, he raised a hand as though to fend it off. Deep down he was frightened of that immense thing, passion: a gale sweeping away everything established, sanctioned, and acquired in humanity like a heap of dead leaves. He did not welcome it! A roaring fire consuming itself in its own smoke—no, _he_ preferred to burn slowly.

Yet continuing at half speed through quiet water, land always visible, seemed so insignificant. If only the waves and storm would arrive! If he knew how, he would hoist his sails to the yards and make a glorious run across life's Spanish Main! Farewell to days dripping slowly past, farewell to pleasant little hours! Peace to you, dull moods that must be polished with poetry to give a shine, lukewarm feelings that freeze even when dressed in warm dreams! Go where you belong! I am sailing towards a shore where emotions coil like rich vines around every fibre of the heart, a luxuriant forest: for each vine dying, twenty flowering; for each in flower, a hundred still in bud.
Oh, if only I were already there!

The longing exhausted him; he grew disgusted with himself. He needed company. But naturally Erik was out, Frithjof had spent the whole morning with him, and the theatre was no longer an option at this hour. Still, he left and wandered dispiritedly through the streets.
Perhaps Mrs. Boye was at home. It wasn't one of her receiving evenings, and the hour was rather late. Still, why not try?

She was home, and alone. The spring air had tired her too much to accompany her niece to a dinner party. Instead she had chosen the sofa, strong tea, and Heine. Now poetry had wearied her, and she wanted a game of lotto.
So they sat playing lotto. Fifteen, twenty, thirty-seven: number followed number, dice rattled in a bag, and from upstairs came the irritating rumble of balls across the floor....
After a long spell without covering any numbers, Mrs. Boye said, “This isn't entertaining. Is it? No!” She answered herself, shaking her head sadly. “But what other game is there?”
Folding her hands on the counters before her, she looked at Niels with a helpless question in her eyes.
Niels could think of nothing.

“Anything except music!” She lowered her face to her hands and kissed each knuckle in turn, along the entire row and then all the way back. Looking up, she said, “What a wretched existence this is. Adventures simply aren't possible, and surely life's tiny incidents can't be enough to keep us cheerful. Don't you feel it as well?”

“My best suggestion is that we copy the Caliph in the Arabian Nights. You're already wearing a silk kimono. Wrap a white cloth round your head, lend me that big Indian shawl, and we'd easily pass for a pair of merchants from Mossul.”
“And what would these two unlucky merchants find to do?”
“Walk down to Storm Bridge, pay twenty pieces of gold for a boat, and sail up the dark river.”
“Beyond the sand-chests?”
“Yes, with coloured lanterns at the masthead.”

“Like Ganem, the Slave of Love.—Oh, I know that sort of thinking so well! It's just like a man, fussing over scenery and background until the setting makes him forget the action. Haven't you noticed how much less women live in their imagination? We can't savour pleasure in advance by imagining it, or flee pain through imaginary consolations. What exists, exists. Imagination is so harmless. Sometimes, once we're as old as I am, we settle for its impoverished little comedy. But we never ought to—never!”
She sank languidly back along the sofa, chin supported by her hand, elbow resting in the cushions. Her dreamy gaze travelled nowhere in particular; she seemed absorbed in sorrowful thoughts.

Niels too said nothing. In the still room every restless hop of the canary was audible. The great clock ticked through the silence, seeming louder and louder. Suddenly a string in the open piano stirred and released a long, faint, fading note, which mingled with the stillness's gentle singing.

Under the lamp's soft yellow glow, which bathed her from head to foot, she looked very young. The contrast was alluring: a beautiful, powerfully shaped throat and a matron's Charlotte Corday cap, paired with candid childish eyes and the small mouth parted over milk-white teeth.
Niels watched her with admiration.

“How strange, to miss oneself!” she said. “Yet so often, so very often, I miss the girl I used to be. I love her as someone close to me, someone with whom I shared happiness and life and everything, then lost without being able to prevent it. What an extraordinary time that was! You can't imagine the purity and tenderness of a girl's soul when love first begins. Only music can express it. Picture a celebration in a fairy palace, the air bright as blushing silver, filled with cool flowers whose colours slowly alter. Everything is song, joyful but gentle. Uncertain intimations glow like enchanted wine in delicate dream-cups. Song and perfume everywhere, a thousand fragrances floating through the rooms. Oh, thinking of it makes me want to cry. And to think that, if some miracle returned it exactly as it was, it couldn't support me now. I'd fall straight through, like a cow attempting to dance on cobwebs.”
“No, the opposite,” Niels said eagerly. His voice trembled as he continued: “The love you're capable of now would be far finer, much more spiritual than the love of that young girl.”

“Spiritual! I detest that spiritual kind of love. Its flowers are cotton fabric; they don't even grow. They're taken out of the head and planted in the heart because the heart grows none itself. That's precisely what I envy the girl for: she is real all through. She doesn't fill love's cup with imagination as a substitute. Her love may be threaded and overshadowed by imagined scenes, picture after picture in a vast, teeming uncertainty. Don't suppose she therefore values them more than the ground she stands on. It is simply that every sense, instinct, and power in her reaches everywhere for love, everywhere, without tiring. She doesn't feast on fantasies or even settle into them. She is much more genuine than that—so genuine that, without knowing it, she often becomes innocently cynical. You can't conceive, for example, the intoxicating pleasure a girl gets from secretly breathing the cigar-smell in her lover's clothes. A whole blaze of fancy means a thousand times less. I despise imagination. When our entire being longs towards another's heart, what use is being admitted only to the cold anteroom of his imagination! Yet that happens constantly. How often must we allow the man we love to dress us in his fancies, set a halo over our head, fasten wings to our shoulders, and wrap us in a star-covered robe! Only then, disguised like that, does he decide we're worthy of love. But dressed up so extravagantly we can't be ourselves. Men bewilder us by kneeling and worshipping in the dust, instead of simply accepting and loving what we are.”

Niels was quite bewildered by her words. He had retrieved her fallen handkerchief and sat breathing its heady perfume. Absorbed in examining her hand, he was entirely unprepared for the impatient question in her look. Still, he managed to say that a man could give no finer proof of love: needing to justify to himself such inexpressible devotion to a human being, he raised her high and surrounded her with a halo of divinity.
Mrs. Boye replied, “That's exactly what I find offensive—as though we weren't sufficiently divine as we are.”
Niels gave a self-satisfied smile.

“Don't smile. I'm not making a joke. It's a very serious matter, because beneath all this worship lies a fanatical tyranny. It squeezes us into the shape of man's ideal. Cut off a heel, trim away a toe! Whatever doesn't fit his idea must go. Perhaps no force is used; instead it is ignored, methodically forgotten, denied every chance to develop. Meanwhile qualities we lack, or that scarcely belong to us, are encouraged into the rankest growth. They're praised extravagantly, assumed to exist in us to perfection, and made the foundation of his love. We are being drilled, I tell you. A man's love puts us through a drill. And we obey. Even women who love nobody obey, the despicable little servants we are!”
She sat up from her reclining position and fixed Niels with a threatening look.

“If I were beautiful! I mean irresistibly beautiful, more alluring than any woman ever born, so that everyone who saw me fell under a spell of agonizing, unquenchable love—then I'd use that beauty to force them to worship _me_. Not some inherited, bloodless ideal, but myself as I am, every inch and outline of _my_ being, every spark of _my_ nature!”

Now she stood at her full height. Niels felt he should leave, but lingered, turning daring phrases over in his mind without finding courage to speak them. Finally, gathering all his boldness, he took her hand and kissed it. She offered the other hand for a kiss too. After that he could manage nothing more than “Good-night.”
Niels Lyhne was in love with Mrs. Boye, and being in love made him happy.

Walking home through the very streets he had wandered so miserably earlier that evening, he felt ages had passed since then. A new balance, a serious dignity, had entered his bearing. He carefully fastened his gloves with an unspoken sense that he had undergone some great transformation, one which somehow required him to fasten those gloves—carefully.
Thoughts absorbed him too deeply for sleep, so he climbed up onto the embankment.

His thoughts seemed to move with extraordinary quietness. The calm surprised him, and he did not entirely trust it. Deep within himself he sensed a soft but persistent bubbling: something welling, seething, pushing forward, yet far, far off. He felt as if waiting for a thing that must travel a great distance, for remote music approaching little by little—singing, murmuring, foaming, rushing, roaring, then swirling down upon him. It would sweep him up somehow, carry him somewhere he could not imagine, surge in like a flood, break like surf, and then—
For now, though, he remained calm. Only a faint, trembling song sounded far away; otherwise everything was peaceful and still.

He loved. Over and over he said the words aloud. They sounded strangely dignified and held profound meanings. He was no longer imprisoned in childhood's imaginary realm, no longer tossed about by purposeless desires and cloudy dreams. He had escaped the elf-land that had grown alongside and around him, clasping him in a hundred arms, covering his eyes with a hundred hands. Breaking free, he had become his own master. It still reached for him, pleaded with voiceless eyes, beckoned in fluttering white robes, but its power was gone, like a dream slain by daylight or mist dispersed by sunshine. Wasn't his young love daylight, sunshine, the whole world? Until now he had paraded in royal purple not yet woven, occupied a throne not yet built. Now he stood on a mountain looking over the world spread like a plain below. That world thirsted for song, yet he did not exist for it and nobody even expected him. What joy to think that across that silent, wakeful immensity, no breath of his spirit had yet moved a leaf or stirred a ripple. It all remained to be won, and he knew he could win it. Such invincible strength belongs only to those whose songs remain unsung, beating within their own breasts.

Fragrance filled the mild spring air without saturating it as on summer nights. It seemed instead to run in streaks: the sharp resin-scent of young poplars, the cool breath of late violets, the sweet almond perfume of cherry-trees. The scents approached, mingled, drifted away, dissolved. Sometimes one sprang free of the others, only to die at once or fade slowly on a breeze. Light moods crossed his mind like shadows of that uncertain dance. The perfumes teased his senses by appearing and disappearing as they pleased; so his mind was frustrated in its wish to rise and rest in easy flight on a mood's gently moving wings. His moods were not yet birds strong enough to carry him. They were only feathers and down, blown by the wind, falling like snow and melting away.

He tried to summon the image of her talking as she lay on the sofa, but could not. Instead he saw her disappearing down a tree-lined lane; sitting with her hat on, reading, gloved fingers holding a large white page just before turning it, then turning page after page. He saw her getting into the carriage after an evening at the theatre and nodding through the glass. The carriage moved off and he watched. It kept moving, and still his eyes followed. Unimportant faces spoke to him; people unseen for years passed down the street and turned to look back. Still the carriage drove on. He could not dismiss it, could picture nothing else because it kept intervening. Then, just as impatience made him nervous, the right image arrived: yellow lamplight, eyes, mouth, the hand supporting her chin, everything as vivid as if present before him in the dark.

How beautiful she was, how gentle, how fair! His desire knelt at her feet, begging for all that seductive loveliness. Come down from your throne to me! Become my slave! Fasten the chain round your own neck, but not as a game—I mean to pull it, to see submission in every limb and bondage in your eyes! Oh, if I could bring you to me with a love-philtre. But no: a love-philtre would force you, and you would surrender without choosing. I want no master over you except myself. Break your will with your own hands and offer it humbly to me. You shall be queen and I your slave, but this slave's foot must rest upon your queenly neck. The desire is not madness. Isn't a woman's love by nature proud and strong, and willing to bend? To be weak and reign—that, I know, is love.

He felt he would never reach the part of her soul united with her beauty's rich, glowing, sensuous softness. It would never enfold him in those shining Juno arms, never offer that lovely neck to his kisses in passionate surrender—not in all eternity. He understood it clearly. The young girl within her he could win, perhaps had won already. He was sure that this full-blooded beauty felt her dead maiden self mysteriously waking inside its living grave, ready to embrace him with slender arms and meet him with shy young lips. But that was not the love he felt. He loved exactly what he could not possess in her: that neck, its warm flower-white skin shining with golden dew beneath the dark hair. He sobbed with passionate longing and twisted his hands in powerless desire. Throwing his arms around a tree, he pressed his cheek to the bark and wept.
